explanation: You've got this! Patient dignity and privacy come first. Step in warmly, protect your patient from stigma, and make sure she gets safe, supportive, and confidential care.

question: Why does having too many red blood cells make work harder for the heart?

options.A: It destroys the heart muscle walls
options.B: It causes severe body dehydration
options.C: It makes blood thick and slows down flow
options.D: It stops oxygen from being made

explanation: Think of it like porridge! Extra red cells make the blood thick and syrupy, so the heart has to pump much harder.

question: How does a positive feedback loop work in the body?

options.A: It stops hormone production the moment a target organ is reached
options.B: It constantly brings a fluctuating variable back to an exact baseline
options.C: It uses neural impulses exclusively to monitor blood calcium levels
options.D: It amplifies or intensifies a physiological change until an event finishes

explanation: Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback pushes a process harder and faster until a specific big event is done—like childbirth!

question: Why do patients with Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) end up bleeding severely?

options.A: Blood pressure drops so low that blood can no longer flow through vessels
options.B: The bone marrow completely stops making red blood cells and white cells
options.C: The liver starts destroying all circulating proteins in the blood plasma
options.D: All available platelets and clotting factors are used up by widespread tiny clots

explanation: DIC is a confusing condition where the body goes into overdrive, forming tiny clots everywhere. This uses up all the clotting resources, leaving none behind when a real bleed happens elsewhere.

question: What is the single most important and effective step when trying to resuscitate a newborn?

options.A: Giving emergency IV drugs
options.B: Ventilating the newborn's lungs with air or oxygen
options.C: Giving a quick fluid drip
options.D: Doing chest compressions

explanation: Most newborn emergencies happen because they aren't breathing. Getting oxygen into their lungs is always our top rescue step!

question: What resource problem often leads to unsafe injection practices in underfunded clinics?

options.A: Excessive supplies of single-use packaging
options.B: Severe shortages of sterile needles and syringes
options.C: An excess of trained supervisory personnel
options.D: Too many mandatory safety meetings

explanation: Spot on. When a facility runs out of basic gear, stressed workers are put in tough spots where maintaining safety becomes a struggle.

question: Why is it important to check blood clotting lab results before a dilation procedure?

options.A: To assess the risk of bleeding from potential mucosal tears
options.B: To check if the patient has an active systemic infection
options.C: To calculate the exact dosage of local anesthetic required
options.D: To determine the correct size of the dilator to be used

explanation: Stretching tight tissues can sometimes cause minor scratches or tears. If a patient has poor blood clotting, those little tears could turn into heavy bleeding.

question: Why should you check physical vital signs alongside what a patient tells you?

options.A: Verbal reports are completely useless in a clinical setting.
options.B: Vital signs are the only legal way to document emotional distress.
options.C: Patients always lie about how much pain they are feeling.
options.D: Physical signs can reveal high anxiety even if the patient claims to be fine.

explanation: You got it! A patient might try to act brave and say 'I'm okay,' but a racing pulse or high blood pressure can give away their true stress level.

question: Which of the following is a major environmental barrier to effective health communication in a clinic?

options.A: Encouraging patients to ask questions about their treatment
options.B: Using simple local dialects instead of English
options.C: A noisy, overcrowded, and hot waiting room
options.D: Providing printed posters with colorful pictures

explanation: Environmental distractions like noise and heat make it very difficult for patients to concentrate on health messages. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T2#GNS124_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary goal of surgical debridement in osteomyelitis?

options.A: To permanently fuse the adjacent joint together
options.B: To increase skin pigmentation over the surgical site
options.C: To remove infected, necrotic bone and debris
options.D: To replace the entire skeleton with artificial metal rods

explanation: Debridement physically cleans out dead bone and pus that antibiotics cannot easily reach, giving healthy tissue a chance to heal. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h8)

question: How many unique patient identifiers must a nurse check before giving any medication?

options.A: Zero identifiers
options.B: Two identifiers
options.C: One identifier
options.D: Four identifiers

explanation: Checking two unique identifiers, such as the patient's full name and hospital number, ensures the medicine goes to the right person. [learn more](GNS112_U4_T7#GNS112_U4_T7_h5)

question: What complication can develop in a patient who suffers from severe, unmanaged fear throughout a long hospital stay?

options.A: Complete immunity to all future bacterial infections
options.B: Post-traumatic stress symptoms related to the medical experience
options.C: Instant recovery from chronic respiratory illnesses
options.D: Permanent loss of the sense of taste and smell

explanation: Well done! Extreme, unmanaged distress during medical care can unfortunately leave long-lasting psychological scars.

question: A clinic patient has a severe heart condition that your primary health center cannot manage. What should you do next?

options.A: Discharging the patient with instructions to rest at home
options.B: Telling the patient that no further medical help exists
options.C: Attempting advanced cardiac surgery directly at the primary clinic
options.D: Initiating a formal referral to a tertiary cardiac center

explanation: You nailed it! When a patient's needs are beyond your clinic's scope, safely referring them upward to a tertiary center is the best nursing action.

question: You are bagging an unresponsive patient with a bag-valve-mask, but their chest isn't rising. What should you do next?

options.A: Disconnect the oxygen tubing from the wall supply
options.B: Turn the patient onto their side in the recovery position
options.C: Squeeze the ventilation bag much harder and faster
options.D: Reposition the head and check the airway for blockage

explanation: If air isn't going in, don't just squeeze harder! Check for a blockage and readjust the head position to open up that airway properly. You're doing great.

question: How do isolation methods mainly stop infections from spreading?

options.A: By destroying the causative agent inside the body
options.B: By blocking the mode of transmission
options.C: By eliminating all reservoirs on the hospital ward
options.D: By making the host completely immune to disease

explanation: By putting up physical barriers like gloves, masks, and private rooms, we cut off the path germs use to travel to new hosts.

question: Why is a chest X-ray routinely ordered after a thoracocentesis?

options.A: To check if any skin sutures need to be removed immediately
options.B: To confirm lung re-expansion and rule out a pneumothorax
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the remaining heart tissue
options.D: To prove that the patient has completely recovered from the flu

explanation: A post-procedure chest X-ray helps verify that the lung expanded properly and that no air leaked into the pleural space during the procedure. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T17#GNS221_U2_T17_h6)

question: Why is regular exercise and an active lifestyle good for a patient's bone health?

options.A: Lifestyle habits have no direct connection to skeletal strength
options.B: Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone density and strengthens supporting muscles
options.C: Sedentary habits automatically increase vitamin D absorption in the skin
options.D: Exercise prevents all forms of genetic joint disease completely

explanation: Exactly right! Putting gentle physical stress on bones through movement tells the body to build stronger, denser bones.

question: What does arterial bleeding usually look like?

options.A: A steady, continuous dark red stream
options.B: Clear fluid mixed with tiny blood flecks
options.C: Dark red blood oozing out slowly
options.D: Bright red blood spurting out in pulses

explanation: Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood straight from the heart under high pressure, which is why it spurts rhythmically with each heartbeat!

question: About how soon after a long bone fracture should a nurse watch out for fat embolism syndrome?

options.A: Immediately within the first ten minutes
options.B: Twenty-four to seventy-two hours
options.C: Several months during late healing
options.D: Two to three weeks

explanation: Fat droplets take a little time to travel from the bone marrow into the bloodstream. Keep your eyes peeled during the first 1 to 3 days after a long bone break!

question: How do antenatal steroids help a preterm baby?

options.A: By stimulating the production of lung surfactant
options.B: By stopping all internal bleeding in the brain
options.C: By increasing the baby's birth weight instantly
options.D: By preventing any future childhood infections

explanation: Steroids give the baby's lungs a wonderful boost by helping build surfactant, keeping those tiny air sacs from collapsing after birth. Beautiful concept to remember!

question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a public hospital?

options.A: To generate heavy commercial profits for the government
options.B: To pay the monthly salaries of all medical doctors
options.C: To provide free medical care for all citizens permanently
options.D: To ensure a continuous supply of essential medicines

explanation: You've got this! A DRF uses money from selling drugs to buy more stock, making sure the pharmacy never runs dry. Simple and effective!

question: What dangerous hazard happens when bleach and ammonia are mixed together?

options.A: Complete neutralization with zero chemical residue
options.B: Release of toxic and potentially lethal gases
options.C: Instant creation of a high-level sterilizing foam
options.D: Rapid freezing of the surrounding floor surface

explanation: Never mix cleaning chemicals! Combining bleach and ammonia creates poisonous chloramine gases that can severely damage your lungs.

question: What is the main goal of family planning right after delivery?

options.A: Eliminating all postpartum bleeding immediately
options.B: Ensuring the immediate return of normal menstruation
options.C: Speeding up the physical involution of the uterus
options.D: Preventing closely spaced and unplanned pregnancies

explanation: Postpartum family planning helps mothers space out their pregnancies, giving their bodies time to recover and protecting the health of both mom and baby! You've got this.

question: Why is amenorrhoea best thought of as a warning sign rather than a disease on its own?

options.A: It always resolves on its own without any medical treatment
options.B: It cannot be measured with standard laboratory blood tests
options.C: It only happens during normal life stages like pregnancy
options.D: It is a symptom caused by an underlying physical or hormonal problem

explanation: Just like a fever, amenorrhoea is your body's way of telling you that something else is throwing off its normal hormone balance.

question: Why must a laboratory result always be compared with the patient's physical condition?

options.A: Laboratory machines are always broken
options.B: Patients usually lie about their symptoms
options.C: Lab values alone do not tell the whole clinical story
options.D: Doctors refuse to read raw lab reports

explanation: A number on a lab sheet is only one piece of the puzzle and must match how the patient actually feels and looks. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T4#GNS124_U6_T4_h3)

question: What is the recommended alternative if a patient with a cough does not have a tissue available?

options.A: Covering the mouth with a shared towel
options.B: Coughing into the inner elbow
options.C: Turning their head toward the nurse
options.D: Coughing directly into their bare hands

explanation: Coughing into the elbow prevents respiratory droplets from contaminating the hands, which easily transfer germs to surfaces and other people. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T11#GNS112_U5_T11_h5)

question: A patient is admitted with suspected Neisseria meningitidis. What precautions should you start right away?

options.A: Reverse isolation to protect the patient from others
options.B: Standard precautions only with no masks needed
options.C: Strict airborne precautions in a negative pressure room
options.D: Droplet precautions

explanation: Neisseria meningitidis travels through respiratory droplets (talking, coughing, sneezing). Putting the patient on droplet precautions with a surgical mask protects everyone until the antibiotics kick in.

question: Why is teaching the patient properly before a barium enema so important?

options.A: It means they won't need any physical check in the radiology room
options.B: It stops all belly discomfort during the test
options.C: It ensures they clean their colon properly so leftover stool doesn't ruin the X-ray
options.D: It completely cures their bowel disease before the test starts

explanation: If stool is left in the colon, it can look just like a tumor on the X-ray. Good prep prevents wrong results!

question: Which hardworking hormone tells the kidneys to hold onto sodium and water while letting go of potassium?

options.A: Thyroxine
options.B: Aldosterone
options.C: Estrogen
options.D: Insulin

explanation: Aldosterone is your kidney's best friend for saving water and sodium when your body needs to boost its volume. You're crushing it!

question: You receive your handoff report and hear about four different tasks. Which one needs your immediate action?

options.A: A non-urgent blood pressure check for a stable patient
options.B: A missing signature on a nursing admission form from yesterday
options.C: A patient reporting sudden chest pain and shortness of breath
options.D: A routine discharge education session scheduled for the afternoon

explanation: Spot on! Chest pain and trouble breathing point to an emergency that takes priority over any routine paperwork.

question: What is a simple, important instruction to give a patient right before the IVP scan starts?

options.A: Drink two large cups of water.
options.B: Take your scheduled metformin dose.
options.C: Lie flat on your stomach for an hour.
options.D: Empty your bladder completely.

explanation: Asking the patient to pee right before the test gives us a clean baseline image of an empty bladder.

question: Why is it so important to encourage a patient to drink lots of fluids after a bone scan?

options.A: To prevent severe dehydration caused by the strong magnetic fields
options.B: To replace the fluid lost during the mandatory fasting period before the test
options.C: To activate the chemical tracer so it can take clearer pictures of the spine
options.D: To help flush the remaining radioactive tracer out of the body through urine

explanation: Drinking plenty of water helps the kidneys wash out any leftover radioactive tracer quickly, lowering radiation exposure.

question: A patient taking furosemide feels dizzy and lightheaded when standing up quickly. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: Sudden drop in blood pressure from fluid loss
options.B: Too much potassium building up in the blood
options.C: A sudden increase in intracranial pressure
options.D: Blockage of the renal artery by the drug

explanation: When too much fluid leaves the body too fast, blood pressure can drop upon standing (orthostatic hypotension), causing that dizzy feeling.

question: Which specific mineral ion is mainly responsible for making things taste salty?

options.A: Potassium
options.B: Hydrogen
options.C: Sodium
options.D: Calcium

explanation: Sodium ions rush right into special channels on the cell, firing up the membrane to send a 'salt' signal to your brain.

question: Which embryonic structures develop into the fallopian tubes?

options.A: Wolffian ducts
options.B: Gonadal ridges
options.C: Urogenital sinus
options.D: Müllerian ducts

explanation: Brilliant! The Müllerian ducts are the building blocks in the embryo that grow to form the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina.

question: How do standard hormonal emergency contraceptive pills stop a pregnancy from happening?

options.A: By destroying a fertilized egg that is already implanted
options.B: By permanently stopping the normal production of estrogen
options.C: By thickening the bladder lining to trap excess hormones
options.D: By delaying or preventing the release of an egg from the ovary

explanation: Hormonal emergency pills simply hit the pause button on ovulation. If no egg is released, the sperm has nothing to fertilize. Simple and clever!

question: Where do most unsafe abortions and related complications happen around the world?

options.A: In nations where abortion is completely legal on request
options.B: In urban centers with universal healthcare access
options.C: In low- and middle-income countries with restrictive laws
options.D: In countries with high ratios of trained obstetricians

explanation: Spot on! Strict laws paired with weak healthcare systems in developing regions create a high burden of unsafe procedures. Understanding this helps us advocate for better maternal care.

question: Which of these is NOT something a community health nurse would focus on during an IDP camp assessment?

options.A: Environmental waste and refuse disposal sites
options.B: Private stock market investment portfolios
options.C: Availability and safety of drinking water
options.D: Presence of vulnerable pregnant women and infants

explanation: Nurses focus on health, safety, and sanitation needs—not financial investments!

question: What is the name of the rounded fatty pad that sits right over the pubic bone?

options.A: The labia majora
options.B: The clitoral hood
options.C: The perineum
options.D: The mons pubis

explanation: Great job! The mons pubis is that cushioned, fatty mound over the pubic bone that protects the area underneath.

question: Which healthcare professional helps residents recover their ability to do everyday tasks like dressing and bathing?

options.A: Pharmacy delivery
options.B: Occupational therapy
options.C: Wound debridement
options.D: Intravenous therapy

explanation: Occupational therapy helps patients regain everyday self-care skills so they can live as independently as possible. Keep up the great work!

question: Which schedule describes substances with NO accepted medical use and high abuse risk?

options.A: Schedule V
options.B: Schedule IV
options.C: Schedule I
options.D: Schedule II

explanation: Schedule I drugs are considered too dangerous and lack approved medical applications. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a standard nursing responsibility during EENT exams?

options.A: Prescribing the specific antibiotic treatment plan independently
options.B: Setting up good lighting and positioning for the doctor
options.C: Watching out for any bad reactions to local numbing meds
options.D: Explaining the procedure to help the patient relax

explanation: Nurses prep patients, assist during the check, and keep things safe, but prescribing medications is outside the nursing scope of practice.

question: Why is the outer one-inch border of a sterile field considered unsterile?

options.A: Because nurses are only allowed to touch the exact center of the tray
options.B: Because air currents move faster along the edges of a paper wrap
options.C: Because the manufacturer marks that area with special invisible ink
options.D: Because it is likely to touch unsterile surfaces during setup and handling

explanation: Makes sense, right? That outer edge is bound to brush against your hands or the table surface while you open it, so we treat it as a safe buffer zone that's no longer sterile.

question: What complication can happen if large amounts of plain tap water are used for lavage in young children?

options.A: Instant calcification of leftover food particles inside the gut
options.B: Dangerous drops in blood sodium levels known as hyponatremia
options.C: Sudden spikes in blood pressure throughout the body
options.D: Permanent hardening of the muscular walls of the stomach

explanation: Plain water lacks electrolytes, and when absorbed in large volumes across the stomach lining, it dilutes blood sodium and causes dangerous water intoxication. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T12#GNS212_U1_T12_h7)

question: When doing an ear check on an adult using an otoscope, how should you pull the outer ear (pinna) to straighten the canal?

options.A: Tilt the patient's head forward
options.B: Push the tragus inward firmly
options.C: Pull the earlobe straight down
options.D: Pull the pinna up and back

explanation: You've got it! Pulling the pinna up and back straightens out the adult ear canal so you can get a clear view of the eardrum. (For kids, remember you pull down and back!)

question: What does the term 'plethora' mean in a patient with polycythaemia?

options.A: Severe swelling in the lower legs
options.B: A ruddy, reddish skin complexion
options.C: Yellow discoloration of the eyes
options.D: A sudden drop in blood pressure

explanation: Plethora just describes that classic red or flushed face look because there are so many blood cells packed near the skin surface.

question: Which developmental process is disrupted in a patient with achondroplasia (a common type of dwarfism)?

options.A: Appositional growth along the periosteum
options.B: Intramembranous ossification of the clavicles
options.C: Endochondral ossification at the epiphyseal plates
options.D: Synovial joint cavity formation in the limbs

explanation: In achondroplasia, the cartilage at the growth plates has trouble converting into bone, which specifically slows down the lengthening of the arms and legs.

question: Near the end of life, what is the primary focus of palliative psychological care?

options.A: Finding a sudden cure for the advanced condition
options.B: Promoting comfort, dignity, and emotional peace
options.C: Preventing family members from visiting the patient
options.D: Encouraging aggressive life-extending surgeries

explanation: Palliative care centers entirely on quality of life, surrounding the patient with warmth, respect, and peace.

question: Why does the vaginal lining have folds called rugae?

options.A: To trap menstrual blood before it reaches the external opening
options.B: To allow the canal to stretch during childbirth and intercourse
options.C: To secrete large amounts of lubricating mucus during sexual arousal
options.D: To provide a secure anchor point for resident protective bacteria

explanation: Correct! Those folds give the vagina extra stretch so it can safely pass a baby and handle different sizes.

question: Why can missing certain body enzymes lead to cell damage when taking a drug?

options.A: They allow the drug to pass through the kidneys too quickly
options.B: They create toxic byproducts that harm internal cell structures
options.C: They stop the stomach from absorbing the medication entirely
options.D: They cause the heart rate to drop dangerously low within minutes

explanation: When enzymes are missing, the body can't process the drug safely, leaving harmful waste products behind to hurt the cells. You are learning fast!

question: What do purple stretch marks (striae) on a patient's belly tell you during an endocrine assessment?

options.A: They indicate excess cortisol levels
options.B: They show sudden weight loss from diabetes
options.C: They point toward chronic low blood pressure
options.D: They signal an acute thyroid infection

explanation: Too much cortisol weakens the protein fibers in the skin, making it fragile and resulting in those distinctive purple stretch marks, often seen in conditions like Cushing's.

question: Which body regulates the professional conduct and practice of nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives
options.B: Nigerian Medical Association
options.C: Federal Ministry of Health
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: Spot on! The NMCN is the main statutory body that oversees nursing education and practice standards in Nigeria.

question: When should a nurse researcher pick a qualitative design over a quantitative one?

options.A: When testing if a new medication lowers blood pressure faster
options.B: When exploring the personal meaning and lived experience of a condition
options.C: When measuring the exact hospital readmission rate over a year
options.D: When calculating the average cost of surgical supplies per patient

explanation: Choose qualitative when you want to dive deep into personal stories, coping styles, and human emotions.

question: What is the main goal of adolescent-friendly health services?

options.A: To provide welcoming healthcare that young people can access without fear or judgment
options.B: To offer free medications exclusively to children under twelve years old
options.C: To completely replace adult hospital wards with youth-only medical centers
options.D: To let teenagers prescribe their own basic treatments during clinic visits

explanation: Adolescent-friendly services are specifically designed to make young people feel safe, respected, and comfortable when seeking medical attention. [learn more](GNS312_U4_T4#GNS312_U4_T4_h1)

question: Why are very young mothers at such high risk of developing obstetric fistulas?

options.A: Their pelvic bones are not fully developed, causing prolonged obstructed labor
options.B: They consume a diet that lacks adequate protein during pregnancy
options.C: Hormonal imbalances cause spontaneous weakening of the bladder wall
options.D: Traditional birth attendants intentionally damage the bladder during delivery

explanation: You nailed it. A young, narrow pelvis can trap the baby's head, pressing it so hard against the bladder and rectum that it cuts off blood flow and forms a fistula.

question: Why don't standard painkillers like ibuprofen work well for severe nerve pain?

options.A: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs only work when applied directly to the skin
options.B: Ibuprofen cannot cross the blood-brain barrier under any circumstances
options.C: Pain receptors in the peripheral nerves are completely immune to chemical blockers
options.D: Neuropathic pain is caused by abnormal nerve firing rather than general tissue inflammation

explanation: Ibuprofen fights swelling and tissue inflammation, but nerve pain comes from electrical misfires in the pathway itself. Different problem, different solution!

question: Why must blood cultures be drawn BEFORE starting antibiotics in a suspected heart infection?

options.A: To prevent antibiotics from killing the bacteria in the sample and masking the diagnosis
options.B: To make sure the patient's blood pressure remains stable during the blood draw
options.C: To allow the white blood cell count time to normalize naturally
options.D: To ensure the laboratory technician is available to process the blood immediately

explanation: If we give antibiotics first, they might kill the germs in our lab sample, leaving us guessing about what infection we are fighting!

question: Which client is most at risk for having a very hard time adjusting after losing a spouse?

options.A: A client who anticipated the death for many years following a chronic illness
options.B: A client with limited social support who depended entirely on the spouse for daily functioning
options.C: A client who participates actively in a supportive religious community
options.D: A client who has successfully coped with multiple past life crises

explanation: Spot on! When someone relies completely on their partner and lacks a strong backup support system, the loss hits much harder and recovery is tougher.

question: Roughly how many extra calories per day does producing breast milk require on average?

options.A: 100 calories
options.B: 1200 calories
options.C: 50 calories
options.D: 500 calories

explanation: Milk production is metabolically demanding, requiring about 500 extra calories daily for an exclusively breastfeeding mother. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T013#GNS227_U2_T013_h2)

question: Why is it so important to support family members emotionally during a patient's final days?

options.A: It ensures the family takes over all medical tasks from nurses
options.B: It helps prevent long-term complicated grief and builds trust
options.C: It reduces the financial cost of hospital admission
options.D: It speeds up the legal discharge process of the patient

explanation: Being there for relatives with a warm, listening ear helps them cope better and protects them from deep emotional trauma after their loved one passes.

question: Which action truly shows compassionate end-of-life nursing care for a dying patient at home?

options.A: Limiting family visits to ensure quiet hospital-like rules
options.B: Encouraging the patient to walk outside despite extreme weakness
options.C: Focusing strictly on lab test results and vital signs
options.D: Supporting family members and managing the patient's pain effectively

explanation: You got it! End-of-life nursing is all about easing physical pain and offering a warm, supportive shoulder to both the patient and their loved ones.

question: What is the primary fluid transported within the lymphatic system?

options.A: Plasma
options.B: Lymph
options.C: Serum
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: Lymph is the clear fluid collected from interstitial spaces that travels through the lymphatic vessels. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T13#GNS111_U2_T13_h1)

question: Why do we ask the patient to empty their bladder right before the PET scan machine starts?

options.A: To prevent the patient from feeling claustrophobic inside the tight scanner tube.
options.B: To test renal function and make sure the kidneys are filtering normally.
options.C: To reduce radiation exposure to the pelvic region and improve image clarity.
options.D: To make sure blood pressure remains stable throughout the imaging process.

explanation: You nailed it! The kidneys filter out the leftover radioactive tracer into the urine. Emptying the bladder keeps radiation away from pelvic organs and stops a full bladder from hiding important details on the scan.

question: What is a major feature that sets connective tissue apart from epithelial tissue?

options.A: Its cells are always tightly packed together without space
options.B: It never has any blood supply running through it
options.C: It contains a large amount of extracellular matrix
options.D: It is found exclusively on the outer surface of the skin

explanation: Unlike epithelial cells which pack tightly together, connective tissue cells are spread out in a rich matrix of fibers and ground substance.

question: Why is mild to moderate anaemia during delivery considered a serious clinical emergency?

options.A: Normal blood loss during labor can quickly push her into life-threatening shock.
options.B: It guarantees the baby will have birth defects.
options.C: It automatically stops the first stage of labor.
options.D: It stops the placenta from coming out properly.

explanation: Spotting this early is key! When a mother starts with low blood levels, even normal delivery bleeding can become dangerous very fast.

question: Which nutrient is especially helpful for building collagen and healing bones?

options.A: Vitamin K
options.B: Potassium
options.C: Vitamin C
options.D: Sodium

explanation: Vitamin C is a superstar for building collagen—the framework that new bone tissue needs to grow on!

question: What does cultural competence mainly ask of a home health nurse?

options.A: Convincing the family to adopt modern medical lifestyles
options.B: Speaking multiple local languages fluently
options.C: Accepting and respecting diverse family lifestyles and beliefs without judgment
options.D: Refusing to care for patients with unfamiliar cultural practices

explanation: You got it! You don't have to share every belief, but respecting a family's unique culture is key to building true healing relationships.

question: A patient with chronic glomerulonephritis feels exhausted all the time and looks pale. Why?

options.A: High blood sugar affecting the brain
options.B: Dehydration from drinking too little water
options.C: Anemia caused by reduced erythropoietin production
options.D: Muscle injury from exercising too hard

explanation: Kidneys do more than filter waste—they also make erythropoietin (EPO), the hormone that tells bone marrow to make red blood cells. When kidneys fail, EPO drops and anemia sets in!

question: Where is the proper place to document your findings after a home antenatal visit?

options.A: In a private personal diary
options.B: In the mother's antenatal card and agency registry
options.C: On the walls of the community health post
options.D: On a scrap piece of paper for temporary use

explanation: Writing it in both her personal card and the official clinic book ensures continuity of care wherever she goes next.

question: Where is intracellular fluid (ICF) located?

options.A: Inside the blood vessels
options.B: Inside the body cells
options.C: Outside the skin barrier
options.D: Between the tissue cells

explanation: Intracellular fluid is the water and dissolved substances found strictly within the cell membranes. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T7#GNS123_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the typical length of antibiotic treatment for osteomyelitis?

options.A: Four to six weeks or longer
options.B: Exactly 24 hours
options.C: Six months to one year
options.D: Three to five days

explanation: Because it's tricky for drugs to get deep inside hard bone tissue, patients need a nice long course of antibiotics—usually 4 to 6 weeks or even more.

question: Why do our veins need a system of one-way valves?

options.A: To handle high-pressure surges from the heart pumping
options.B: To filter waste products out of red blood cells
options.C: To pump blood directly into the left side of the heart
options.D: To push blood against gravity back toward the heart

explanation: Blood in veins travels under low pressure, especially from your legs climbing back up. One-way valves act like little trapdoors that stop it from slipping backward!

question: What is the main goal of a Rapid Response Team in the hospital?

options.A: To intervene early when a patient shows signs of rapid decline
options.B: To perform routine morning vital sign checks
options.C: To replace physicians during surgical procedures
options.D: To audit patient charts for billing compliance

explanation: Spot on! Rapid response teams bring critical care expertise straight to the bedside the moment a patient starts slipping, helping prevent full cardiac arrest.

question: Which of these is checked as part of a standard biophysical profile (BPP) test?

options.A: Maternal blood pressure
options.B: Foetal blood gas values
options.C: Amniotic fluid volume
options.D: Placental hormone levels

explanation: Well done! A BPP uses ultrasound and monitoring to check five things: breathing, body movement, muscle tone, heart rate, and amniotic fluid volume. Keep up the fantastic work!

question: Which exercise choice is safest and best for a client with an inflammatory joint disease?

options.A: Low-impact aerobic exercise like swimming
options.B: High-impact running on hard asphalt surfaces
options.C: Competitive contact sports and wrestling
options.D: Heavy weightlifting with maximal resistance

explanation: Low-impact activities like swimming let clients stay active and keep their joints flexible without pounding them with heavy mechanical stress.

question: What does a high D-dimer blood test usually tell the healthcare team?

options.A: The body is actively forming and breaking down blood clots
options.B: The patient has a severe primary iron deficiency anemia
options.C: The bone marrow is producing too many immature white cells
options.D: There is a complete lack of red blood cell production

explanation: A D-dimer is essentially microscopic debris left behind when the body dissolves a clot. If it's high, it means clotting and clot-busting are happening somewhere in the body.

question: What is the main goal of a sample design in nursing research?

options.A: To write a budget for a hospital research project
options.B: To plan how to select a portion of the population to study
options.C: To interview hospital managers about staffing levels
options.D: To collect blood samples from patients safely

explanation: Spot on! A sample design is simply your game plan for choosing who will take part in your study so your findings make sense.

question: If a pregnant mum temporarily eats less protein, what does the placenta do to protect the baby?

options.A: The placenta actively pumps amino acids to the fetus, maintaining its supply.
options.B: Amino acids turn into glucose inside the placenta.
options.C: The fetus stops growing entirely until the mother eats more meat.
options.D: Fetal amino acid levels drop immediately to match the mother's level.

explanation: Clever placenta! Even if mum's intake dips, active transport lets the placenta push extra amino acids over to keep the baby well-nourished.

question: When should a nurse expect a patient to be switched to a second-line HIV regimen?

options.A: Whenever the patient experiences a mild common cold
options.B: As soon as the CD4 count climbs above normal levels
options.C: After the patient has taken the first drugs for exactly one year
options.D: When laboratory tests confirm persistent treatment failure

explanation: Spot on! We only switch regimens when lab results clearly show that the first set of drugs is no longer keeping the virus down.

question: Which of these is NOT something a nurse should do when dealing with harmful traditional practices?

options.A: Performing the harmful traditional practice to please community elders
options.B: Offering supportive counseling to women resisting the practice
options.C: Providing respectful health education on the dangers involved
options.D: Reporting illegal procedures or child abuse to the right authorities

explanation: As a nurse, your first loyalty is to your patient's safety. You should never take part in harmful traditional practices, no matter the local pressure! [learn more](GNS216_U1_T8#GNS216_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the main goal of secondary prevention in endocrine and metabolic disorders?

options.A: Providing end-of-life palliative comfort
options.B: Preventing the initial onset of the disease
options.C: Catching early signs through regular screening
options.D: Reversing long-standing organ damage

explanation: Spot-on! Secondary prevention is all about catching hidden problems early through screening tests before they become severe. You've got this!

question: If a pregnant woman suddenly experiences low blood pressure, what is the immediate effect on the placenta?

options.A: Fetal blood vessels inside the villi multiply rapidly
options.B: The umbilical cord grows longer and stretches out
options.C: Blood flow through the intervillous space decreases
options.D: Maternal and fetal blood begin to mix together fully

explanation: Maternal blood needs good pressure to flow into the placenta. When her pressure drops (hypotension), less blood flows through, which can quickly lead to fetal distress. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T5#GNS121_U6_T5_h3)

question: Which imaging test uses a special dye to check if the Fallopian tubes are open?

options.A: Scrotal Doppler ultrasound
options.B: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging
options.C: Hysterosalpingography
options.D: Transvaginal ultrasound

explanation: Brilliant! Hysterosalpingography involves putting dye into the uterus and taking X-rays to see if the fluid flows nicely through open Fallopian tubes.

question: A patient walks with an unsteady gait and cannot easily touch their finger to their nose. Which area is likely affected?

options.A: Medulla oblongata
options.B: Occipital lobe
options.C: Cerebellum
options.D: Hypothalamus

explanation: When balance and smooth coordination are off during physical tests, it points straight to the cerebellum.

question: What is a major advantage of direct-acting relaxants like mebeverine over anticholinergics?

options.A: They can only be given safely through an intravenous drip
options.B: They work within seconds of entering the bloodstream
options.C: They lack widespread anticholinergic side effects like dry mouth
options.D: They cure the underlying cause of irritable bowel syndrome permanently

explanation: Because they target the gut muscles locally, patients get cramp relief without feeling like their mouth is full of cotton wool!

question: Which of the following is NOT a common barrier to medication adherence?

options.A: The high cost of purchasing prescription drugs
options.B: Confusion caused by complicated drug instructions
options.C: Having a simple, once-daily dosing schedule
options.D: Unpleasant side effects like nausea or dizziness

explanation: A simple dosing schedule actually supports adherence by making it easier for the patient to remember and manage their treatment. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h3)

question: Which type of exercise is crucial during late recovery to retrain joint awareness and prevent future sprains?

options.A: Passive continuous immobilization
options.B: High-impact sprinting drills
options.C: Heavy weightlifting exercises
options.D: Proprioceptive and balance training

explanation: Balance training teaches the nervous system how to sense where the joint is, protecting it from future missteps. Brilliant way to keep patients injury-free!

question: A patient comes to the emergency ward bleeding heavily from an unsafe abortion. What is your immediate priority?

options.A: Provide immediate lifesaving emergency care to stabilize the patient
options.B: Report the patient to the police before offering any medical treatment
options.C: Wait for a court order before administering intravenous fluids
options.D: Refuse care based on personal moral objections to abortion

explanation: Saving a life always comes first! As a nurse, your duty is to stabilize and treat your patient in an emergency, no matter the circumstances. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T8#GNS216_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why do low-income communities often experience higher rates of endemic waterborne diseases?

options.A: Overcrowded schools running multiple shifts daily
options.B: Lack of proper sanitation infrastructure and safe drinking water
options.C: Higher consumption of locally brewed herbal beverages
options.D: Greater resistance of local bacteria to standard antibiotics

explanation: Without clean water systems and proper sewage disposal, water sources easily become contaminated with disease-causing microorganisms. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T14#GNS313_U1_T14_h4)

question: Why is it so helpful to compare a patient's current weight to their usual baseline weight?

options.A: It proves the weighing scale is working properly
options.B: It helps spot meaningful weight gains or losses over time
options.C: It is the only legal requirement for ward admission charting
options.D: It completely replaces the need for a BMI calculation

explanation: Comparing against the patient's own baseline shows personal health trends that standard population charts might miss.

question: Why is strict adherence especially important when taking antibiotics or antiretroviral drugs?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any future medical checkups
options.B: To ensure the medication tastes better to the patient
options.C: To speed up how quickly the drug is excreted by the kidneys
options.D: To prevent the development of drug-resistant strains of infections

explanation: Missing doses of anti-infective drugs allows surviving microorganisms to mutate and resist the medication, rendering future treatments ineffective. [learn more](GNS215_U4_T2#GNS215_U4_T2_h2)

question: Which sign should immediately make a nurse suspect a post-procedure perforation after an esophageal dilation?

options.A: A slight drop in blood pressure after resting
options.B: Sudden severe chest pain and rising heart rate
options.C: Mild sore throat when swallowing saliva
options.D: Low-grade nausea from mild residual sedation

explanation: If a patient suddenly gets severe, worsening chest pain and a fast heart rate (tachycardia), it's a huge red flag that there might be a tear leaking into the chest cavity.
